title: Multicast DNS

hero.subtitle: Zero-configuration DNS resolution on local networks using multicast

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Multicast DNS (mDNS) enables DNS-like name resolution on local networks without a dedicated DNS server. Devices query and respond using IP multicast, making it possible to discover services and resolve names in a zero-configuration environment.

mDNS is the technology behind Apple's Bonjour, Linux's Avahi, and similar zero-config networking implementations. It enables devices to automatically discover printers, file shares, and other services on the local network.
sections.eli5: Normally computers ask a big phone book to find each other. In a small network there is no phone book, so they just call out a name and the right one answers.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
mDNS uses the same DNS message format (RFC 1035) but sends queries and responses to a well-known multicast address instead of a unicast DNS server:

IPv4 Multicast Address224.0.0.251
IPv6 Multicast Addressff02::fb
UDP Port5353
Domain.local
No Server Required
Every device on the network acts as both client and server. Any device can claim a name and respond to queries for that name.
Link-Local Scope
mDNS uses link-local multicast addresses, and responses are sent with an IP TTL of 255; a host only accepts responses to its queries that originate from the local link. This is by design — mDNS is intended for local service discovery.
sections.eli5: Everyone listens on the same shared channel. You call out a name to the whole room, and the one who owns the name speaks up. The call does not leave the room.

sections.title: .local Domain
sections.content:
mDNS uses the .local pseudo-top-level domain. Any DNS query for a name ending in .local is resolved via multicast rather than conventional unicast DNS.

mDNS Name Examples
mycomputer.local.        A      192.168.1.100
myprinter.local.         A      192.168.1.50
nas-backup.local.        A      192.168.1.200
_http._tcp.local.        PTR    My Web Server._http._tcp.local.
_printer._tcp.local.     PTR    Office Printer._printer._tcp.local.

The .local domain should not be used in unicast DNS. Conflicts between mDNS and unicast DNS for .local names can cause resolution failures, particularly in enterprise environments using .local for Active Directory domains.
sections.eli5: Any name that ends in .local is a name for the room you are in, so it is answered by shouting instead of by looking it up in the phone book.

sections.title: Record Types
sections.content:
mDNS supports all standard DNS record types. The most commonly used types in mDNS are:

AIPv4 address for a .local hostname
AAAAIPv6 address for a .local hostname
PTRService instance enumeration (browsing)
SRVService instance location (host and port)
TXTService metadata (key-value pairs)
sections.eli5: The answers come in the same kinds of cards as the normal phone book: one with the number, one with a service's place, and one with extra notes.

sections.title: Conflict Resolution
sections.content:
When a device joins the network or claims a new name, it must verify that the name is not already in use:

Probing
Before claiming a name, the device sends three probe queries at 250ms intervals, asking if anyone else owns that name. If no conflict is detected, the name is claimed.
Announcing
After successfully probing, the device announces its records by multicasting them to all peers. This populates other devices' caches.
Conflict Handling
If a conflict is detected (two devices claiming the same name), the device picks a new name, for example by appending the digit 2, and probes again: mycomputer.local might become mycomputer-2.local.
sections.eli5: Before keeping a name, a computer asks three times whether anyone else already has it. If someone does, it picks a new name, like adding a 2 on the end.

references.text: Cheshire, S. and M. Krochmal, "DNS-Based Service Discovery", RFC 6763, February 2013.

subtitle: Zero-configuration DNS resolution on local networks using multicast

eli5.summary: When you walk into a room and want to find the printer, you ask out loud, and the printer answers for itself. No receptionist is needed.

questions: what happens when two devices use the same mdns name

tldr.problem: Small or unmanaged networks have no DNS server, yet devices still need to find each other by name.
tldr.mechanism: Hosts send ordinary DNS-format queries to a multicast address, and the host that owns the name answers for itself.
tldr.outcome: Names ending in .local resolve with no configuration and no server, but only on the local link.

today: mDNS is widely deployed in home and office networks: Apple's Bonjour, Avahi on Linux and the Windows resolver all speak it, and printers, speakers, TVs and phones use it to advertise themselves. Combined with DNS-Based Service Discovery (RFC 6763) it is how AirPrint and Chromecast-style discovery work.
